title: Ultra-poor savers' bank deposits fall Tk 19 crore in three months
excerpt: Ultra-poor people's no-frills bank accounts lost 6.43% of deposits in July-September and safety-net accounts lost Tk 102 crore, Bangladesh Bank data show.

image.alt: The front of a state-owned Agrani Bank branch in Chattogram
image.credit: File photo: Moheen Reeyad / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content:
DHAKA, 28 November 2026: Savings in special bank accounts held by ultra-poor people fell by about Tk 19 crore in the three months to September, even as more of these accounts were opened, Prothom Alo reported on Friday (27 November), citing Bangladesh Bank's latest quarterly report on "no-frills" accounts.

No-frills accounts can be opened with Tk 10, Tk 50 or Tk 100. They need no minimum balance, carry no service charges and can pay more interest than ordinary savings accounts. Bangladesh Bank introduced them to bring low-income and marginalised people into the banking system. The report covers July to September 2026.

The more than 3.5 million accounts for ultra-poor people held about Tk 273 crore at the end of September, down from Tk 292 crore at the end of June, a fall of 6.43%. Over the same period the number of these accounts rose by more than 24,000, so the average balance dropped from Tk 833 to Tk 774.

Accounts for beneficiaries of government social safety net programmes, such as old-age and widow allowances, are the largest group, at about 10.9 million. Their deposits fell by more than Tk 102 crore in three months, the biggest single reason for the overall decline, the newspaper said. Across all no-frills accounts, deposits fell by more than Tk 121 crore (2.21%) to about Tk 5,370 crore, while the number of accounts grew by about 25,000 to nearly 29.6 million. The average balance fell from Tk 1,858 to Tk 1,816.

Garment workers were the exception. Their roughly 1.32 million Tk 100 accounts held about Tk 546 crore, up more than Tk 27 crore in the quarter, an average of Tk 4,123. Farmers hold more than 10.7 million Tk 10 accounts but only about Tk 792 crore in them, an average of Tk 738.

Experts told Prothom Alo that low-income people may be drawing on savings to meet living costs. Bangladesh Bank recommended reactivating long-dormant accounts, encouraging regular saving, designing savings and credit products for farmers' seasonal incomes, and raising awareness among women, young people and older people.

Why it matters

Safety-net allowances are paid into these accounts, so falling balances suggest that recipients withdraw almost everything they receive and have little left to save. That fits other signs of strain on poor households, from the World Bank's finding that half of the poorest households get no safety net to the central bank's annual financial inclusion report. Opening accounts is not the same as financial inclusion: programmes that pay cash or promote savings groups may need to track whether people can keep any money in them.

What to watch

  • Whether balances recover in Bangladesh Bank's October-December report.
  • Any Bangladesh Bank steps to reactivate dormant accounts or launch farmer-focused savings products.
  • How the Family Card pilot pays its allowances and whether it uses these accounts.

Sources

  • Prothom Alo: Savings in ultra-poor people's bank accounts fall by Tk 19 crore in three months (Bangla), 27 November 2026
